paper.title: A Commuting Model
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement. The paper states only that 'The data used in the analyses of commuting stem from Statistics Denmark' and that register addresses of residence and workplace are known for all employed; …

registers.role: outcome / sample frame: addresses of residence and of workplace for all employed, aggregated to the municipality-pair commuting matrix
treatment construction: road-network distances between municipalities, used to build the distance and commuting-cost matrices
controls: municipality characteristics used in the logit model (the paper says the variables stem from different sources, e.g. this one)

linkages: Individual employed persons link a workplace municipality a to a residence municipality b through their register addresses; records are aggregated to municipality level for each sector, giving the commuting matrix q_ab
Municipality-level characteristics (housing costs, forest, tax, social security recipients) are merged onto the residence municipality b
Municipality pairs are linked to a road-network distance matrix (Vejdirektoratet 1994) and to the derived commuting-cost matrix c_ab

sample.universe: All employed persons in Denmark in 1995 for whom the register addresses of residence and of workplace are known
sample.unit_of_observation: Municipality pair (workplace municipality a, residence municipality b); the underlying records are employed individuals, aggregated to municipality level for each sector
selection_rules: All employed persons, with addresses of residence and workplace known from the registers
Data aggregated to municipality level for each sector
Sector dimension suppressed in the reported estimations ('for all employees aggregated')
Figure 2 only: observations grouped into intervals of two kilometres, and only observations less than 60 km included

construction_notes: Spatial separation measured with a road-network distance matrix: a Pascal programme divides Denmark, as well as a minor part of Sweden, into eight parts within each of which a journey can be made crossing land only; for municipalities separated by water all possible routes are evaluated and the cheapest/shortest is assumed.

Intra-municipality distances are set to 2/3 times the square root of the radius for a circle with the same area as the municipality - the mean distance of trips to the centre for origins evenly spread out at the circle.

Commuting cost matrix c_ab: distances by land weighted by the cost per kilometre of driving a car, set with a rough estimate to 1 DKK (Rasmussen 1996); distances by sea priced at the fare for bringing a car with a driver; costs modified according to the Danish tax rules for deductions for commuters. The resulting costs matrix fits car traffic only.
For the necessary/wasteful commuting decomposition distances (not costs) are used, and distances by land and by sea are treated equally.

Average commuting distance 15.8 km; necessary commuting found by minimizing total travel costs subject to constraints securing the marginal sums; wasteful commuting is the residual (8.8 km per employee, 56% of total commuting).
In the logit model, commuting costs and housing costs are measured in 100 DKK, and forest, tax and social security recipients in per cent (Table 2, column 'Unit').
Table 2 reports t-values in parentheses, not standard errors; goodness of fit is reported as pseudo R2 = 0.59 and rho2 = 0.69.

claims.statement: In a logit model of residential location choice for employed persons in Denmark in 1995, commuting costs (100 DKK) enters the utility of living in municipality b with a negative coefficient, so the probability that someone working in municipality a lives in municipality b falls with it.

register_source.value: Not a register variable: built from road-network distances (Vejdirektoratet 1994, Vejafstande i Danmark) and a cost per kilometre of 1 DKK (Rasmussen 1996), modified by Danish commuter tax-deduction rules

definition.value: Cost of commuting between workplace municipality a and residence municipality b, from the c_ab cost matrix: road-network distances (Vejdirektoratet 1994) weighted by the cost per kilometre of driving a car, set to 1 DKK/km (Rasmussen 1996); for distances by sea the price of bringing a car with a driver; costs further modified according to the Danish tax rules for deductions for commuters; intra-municipality distances set to 2/3 times the square root of the radius of a circle with the same area as the municipality. Entered in units of 100 DKK. It varies with both the workplace and the residence municipality (one of the first I1 variables of equation (7)).

timing.value: Measured for 1995, the year of the data; cross-sectional, contemporaneous with the observed residence-workplace pattern

outcome.label: Probability p_a(b) that an individual who works in municipality a chooses municipality b as municipality of residence

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark registers: addresses of residence and of workplace for all employed (the specific register is not named); aggregated to municipality level for each sector

definition.value: The logit choice probability of equation (6), p_a(b-bar) = exp(V_a(b-bar)) / SUM_b exp(V_a(b)): the probability of choosing the specific municipality b-bar for residence for an individual who works in municipality a. Empirically it is the share of the employees working in municipality a who live in municipality b, from the register-based municipality-pair matrix for 1995.

units.value: change in the deterministic utility V_a(b) of residing in municipality b per 100 DKK of commuting cost (logit coefficient; Table 2 reports the unit as '100 DKK')

magnitude.interpretation: Table 2 reports a corresponding elasticity of -0.62 for this variable.

estimand.target_population: Employed persons in Denmark in 1995 ('for all employees aggregated'), choosing a municipality of residence given their workplace municipality

population.description: All employed persons in Denmark in 1995 for whom the register addresses of residence and of workplace are known; the data are aggregated to municipality level for each sector, and the estimation is run for all employees aggregated
population.selection: Employed persons only, and only those whose addresses of residence and of workplace are known from the registers; observations aggregated to municipality pairs

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across Danish municipality pairs in 1995 in commuting costs and in characteristics of the potential residence municipality. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used: identification rests on the random-utility (logit) model imposed on the observed residence-workplace matrix.

key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals choose the alternative which yields the highest utility, and the stochastic parts of utility mu_ab are independent and identically distributed with the Weibull distribution (which delivers the logit form)
The deterministic part of utility V_a(b) is a linear function of the characteristics of the choice

formal.as_written: V_a(b) = SUM_{i=1}^{I_1} beta_i x_ib|a + SUM_{i=I_1+1}^{I} beta_i x_ib   (7)

key_assumptions.assumption: The parameters in the utility function are equal for all workplace municipalities

The explanatory variables included in the utility function are uncorrelated with the stochastic part of utility mu_ab, i.e. no relevant variable is omitted or misspecified; the paper concedes this may fail
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test. The paper discusses it as a threat: it says lack of data is a major reason for exclusion of relevant variables and that exclusion or misspecification influences the error terms.

given: Dummy (variable not defined in the paper)

key_assumptions.assumption: Independence of irrelevant alternatives: the ratio of two residence-choice probabilities does not depend on the other municipalities available, as implied by the i.i.d. Weibull errors

threats_discussed: Exclusion or misspecification of explanatory variables as a source of bias (the paper cites Anas 1982 listing ten major sources of bias, among them the specification of the choice model, the specification of the utility function and data measurement methods)
Measurement of spatial separation: the ad hoc definition of intra-municipality distances and the fact that distances between neighbouring municipalities can be much shorter than measured
The resulting costs matrix fits car traffic only and is used as a proxy for general travel costs
Some employees are registered in another municipality than they actually work in, and some individuals live far from their workplace and probably commute only in weekends
robustness_checks: Two measures of fit are reported: pseudo R2 = 0.59 and rho2 = 0.69 (Table 2)
Elasticities are reported alongside the parameters, because the size of the parameters is difficult to judge directly
unresolved_confounders: Relevant explanatory variables excluded for lack of data: 'The selection of the explaining variables is characterised as an important source of bias. Exclusion or misspecification influences the error terms.'

estimation.specification: Logit residential-location choice model, equations (6) and (7): the deterministic utility of living in municipality b for an individual working in municipality a is linear in commuting costs, a dummy, housing costs, share of forest, local tax level and share of social security recipients, with no constant; probabilities given by equation (6).

source_table.value: Table 2 ('Estimation results and elasticities, logit model'), column 'Logit model', row 'Commuting costs'

definition.value: The c_ab cost matrix used for calibration: distances by land follow the road network and are weighted by the cost per kilometre of driving a car (1 DKK/km); distances by sea are priced at the fare for bringing a car with a driver; costs are modified according to the Danish tax rules for deductions for commuters; individuals are assumed to choose the cheapest/shortest route; intra-municipality distances are set to 2/3 times the square root of the radius for a circle with the same area as the municipality.

key_assumptions.assumption: The register measure of the municipality pair is the commuting relation of interest; the paper concedes some employees are registered in another municipality than they actually work in, and that some individuals living far from their workplace probably commute only in weekends
key_assumptions.supported_by: No correction is made; the paper refers to Miljoeministeriet (1994).

ambiguities: The paper prints the calibrated equation, not a coefficient table: the recorded point estimate -2.41 is the number as printed in the exponent of equation (9). In the notation of equation (4) the parameter is gamma = 2.41 (positive by construction, because the model is written with a minus sign).
No uncertainty of any kind is printed for the gravity parameters, so statistically_significant is left null rather than set to true or false.

The paper does not state how the gravity parameter itself was calibrated (only that the balancing constants are found iteratively, and that logit maximum-likelihood estimates correspond to the gravity values as shown by Anas 1983).

evidence.how: The point estimate recorded is the coefficient on c_ab exactly as printed in the exponent of equation (9): c_ab^-2.41. In the notation of equation (4), where the model is written q_ab = A_a B_b O_a D_b c_ab^-gamma, this corresponds to gamma = 2.41.

value.normalisation: Doubly constrained: the balancing constants A_a and B_b are chosen so that the marginal sums reproduce the given day population O_a and night population D_b. The sector dimension e is suppressed ('for all employees aggregated').

claims.statement: Actual commuting in Danish municipalities in 1995 exceeds the cost-minimising (necessary) commuting implied by the observed day and night populations: the residual, wasteful commuting, averages 8.8 kilometres per employee and makes up 56% of total commuting.

treatment.label: Necessary commuting: the commuting pattern minimising total travel costs subject to constraints securing the day and night populations

register_source.value: Derived, not a register variable: computed from the municipality day and night populations (register addresses of workplace and of residence) and the road-network distance matrix

definition.value: The necessary commuting is found by minimizing total travel costs, given constraints securing the marginal sums (the day population O_a and the night population D_b). The above described distance matrix is used; for this comparison distances by land and by sea are treated equally.

outcome.label: Wasteful commuting, kilometres per employee (actual commuting minus necessary commuting)

register_source.value: Derived, not a register variable: actual commuting distance per employee from the register-based municipality-pair matrix and the distance matrix, minus the computed necessary commuting

definition.value: Wasteful commuting is the residual when the necessary commuting is subtracted from the actual commuting. Table 1 reports it in total kilometres and in average kilometres per employee for Danish municipalities in 1995.

units.value: kilometres per employee (Table 1, row 'Average (kilometres per employee)', column 'Wasteful')

magnitude.interpretation: The wasteful commuting constitutes 56% of the total amount of commuting.

population.description: All employed persons in Denmark in 1995 for whom the register addresses of residence and of workplace are known, aggregated to Danish municipalities
population.selection: Employed persons only, and only those whose addresses of residence and of workplace are known from the registers

identification.source_of_variation: None: an accounting decomposition. Actual commuting in the 1995 register matrix is compared with the cost-minimising assignment of the same day and night populations.

key_assumptions.assumption: The necessary commuting is the solution of minimizing total travel costs given constraints securing the marginal sums (day and night populations)

For the necessary/wasteful decomposition, distances by land and by sea are treated equally, even though sea distances could be argued to deserve a higher weight because of higher energy consumption per person on a ferry
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the objection and says it is ignored here.

key_assumptions.assumption: Intra-municipality distances are set to 2/3 times the square root of the radius for a circle with the same area as the municipality
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes that short commuting distances are encumbered with uncertainty because of this ad hoc definition.

key_assumptions.assumption: Jobs and houses are treated as fully substitutable in the cost-minimising benchmark; the paper notes this is not true in practice (few jobs and houses available at a point in time, couples constrained in their residence choice, heterogeneous housing and labour markets), which is why wasteful commuting exists
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussed in the text, not tested.

threats_discussed: The ad hoc definition of intra-municipality distances makes short commuting distances uncertain
Distances by sea are not weighted higher than distances by land, though energy consumption per person is higher on a ferry
